title: Episode 37: The Galloping Gertie Disaster: Tacoma Narrows
description:
On November 7, 1940, the four-month-old Tacoma Narrows suspension bridge in Washington began violently twisting in a forty-two-mile-per-hour wind. Undulating like a roller coaster with vertical waves of up to twenty-eight feet, the two-thousand-eight-hundred-foot span dramatically tore itself apart and plummeted into Puget Sound, captured on iconic color film and changing suspension bridge design forever.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the summer of nineteen forty, the state of Washington celebrated the grand opening of an architectural marvel: the Tacoma Narrows Bridge. Spanning the swift, churning waters of Puget Sound, it was the third-longest suspension bridge in the world, an exquisite, slender ribbon of steel and concrete hailed as the pinnacle of modern structural engineering. But from the day it opened, the bridge had an alarming, unnatural personality: whenever the wind blew, the roadway began to rise and fall in giant, rolling waves, earning the affectionate nickname 'Galloping Gertie.' Thrill-seeking motorists drove from miles around to ride the bucking bridge like an amusement park roller coaster. But on a howling November morning, the gentle roller coaster transformed into a violent, twisting monster of steel that tore itself apart before the horrified eyes of onlookers. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE SLENDER JEWEL OF THE SOUND
In the late nineteen thirties, the Puget Sound region was booming with naval yards, timber mills, and commerce, but the Kitsap Peninsula was cut off from the mainland city of Tacoma by the treacherous tidal waters of the Tacoma Narrows. Travelers faced long, inconvenient ferry rides across the strait. To bridge the gap, the Washington Toll Bridge Authority commissioned a magnificent suspension bridge. Designed by renowned consulting engineer Leon Moisseiff—one of the leading bridge engineers in the world who had worked on the Golden Gate Bridge—the Tacoma Narrows Bridge was a masterpiece of cutting-edge nineteen thirties design theory. Moisseiff championed the 'deflection theory,' which posited that suspension cables themselves provided immense stiffness, allowing bridge designers to make the deck structure far lighter, cheaper, and more aesthetically slender. Rather than using deep, open steel trusses that allowed wind to pass through, Moisseiff specified solid steel plate girders just eight feet deep, creating a sleek, elegant span two thousand eight hundred feet long between towers. Completed at a cost of six million dollars, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened with grand fanfare on July first, nineteen forty, connecting communities and hailed as an engineering triumph. Connecting the Olympic Peninsula with the bustling mainland was an engineering dream dating back to the late nineteenth century, promising to accelerate timber transport and naval traffic around Puget Sound. Ferry crossings across the windy Tacoma Narrows had been plagued by delay and mechanical breakdowns for decades, leading civic leaders to demand a permanent steel crossing that could unite the region.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE BIRTH OF GALLOPING GERTIE
Yet even during its construction, steelworkers on the high iron noticed something unsettling. Whenever a moderate breeze blew through the Tacoma Narrows, the roadway didn't merely sway sideways—it undulated vertically, rising and falling in rhythmic, undulating ripples like a sea serpent. Construction workers nicknamed the bridge 'Galloping Gertie,' and many suffered from severe bouts of motion sickness while working on the deck. When the bridge opened to the public, the phenomenon became a national curiosity. Drivers reported that as they crested a wave on the deck, the car in front of them would completely disappear into a trough, only to reappear seconds later. Rather than scaring people away, Gertie became a major tourist attraction: families drove onto the bridge on breezy weekends to experience the thrilling sensation of driving across a bucking mechanical wave. Bridge authorities installed hydraulic shock absorbers and heavy tie-down cables to anchor the bridge, but the rolling waves persisted, and engineers from the University of Washington set up cameras and instruments to study the bridge's strange dynamics. Renowned consulting engineer Leon Moisseiff championed the slender eight-foot solid steel plate girders, arguing that modern deflection theory made heavy open-web trusses obsolete, a design philosophy that prioritized visual elegance over aerodynamic stability. Construction workers nicknamed the bridge Galloping Gertie during assembly, feeling the slender steel roadway undulating beneath their feet even in gentle four-mile-an-hour sea breezes.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE FATAL MORNING OF NOVEMBER 7
The breaking point arrived on the morning of Thursday, November seventh, nineteen forty. A blustery autumn cold front swept in from the Pacific Ocean, channeling sustained winds of forty-two miles per hour straight through the Tacoma Narrows gorge. Around seven-thirty in the morning, Galloping Gertie began undulating violently in its familiar vertical wave pattern, rising and falling in eight separate nodes with amplitudes of up to five feet. Motorists who attempted to cross found the ride terrifying; cars bottomed out, and drivers gripped their steering wheels in panic. Around ten o'clock in the morning, a sudden, catastrophic shift occurred in the bridge's mechanical behavior. A heavy steel cable band connecting a suspension cable to the center of the span snapped with a loud gunshot crack. Deprived of its symmetrical balance, the bridge's motion instantly transformed from a harmless vertical wave into a terrifying torsional flutter: the two sides of the deck began twisting violently in opposite directions around the center line. Local motorists drove across the bridge specifically for the thrill of experiencing the vertical roller-coaster motion, with waves rising and falling ten feet as cars appeared and disappeared from view on the rolling deck. Toll collectors on the bridge approaches warned drivers to proceed slowly, while photographers set up tripods on the bluffs to capture pictures of the undulating concrete waves rolling along the main span.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE TWISTING MONSTER
The twisting motion was monstrous and apocalyptic. The bridge roadway tilted up to forty-five degrees from horizontal, twisting back and forth like a giant ribbon of licorice. One sidewalk would rise twenty-eight feet into the air while the opposite sidewalk plummeted twenty-eight feet below. Concrete light poles snapped off like matchsticks; steel rivets popped from their joints with deafening bangs and shot through the air like rifle bullets. On the center of the span was an abandoned black Buick sedan belonging to Leonard Coatsworth, a copy editor for the Tacoma News Tribune. Coatsworth had been driving across the bridge with his wife's pet dog, a black cocker spaniel named Tubby, in the back seat. When the violent twisting began, Coatsworth's car was tossed sideways against the steel curb, its windows shattering. Terrified for his life, Coatsworth scrambled out of the window, crawled on his hands and knees along the tilted, buckling deck, clawing at the steel expansion joints with bloody knuckles, and miraculously reached the safety of the east tower. Tubby remained trapped in the bucking car, too terrified to move. Motorists abandoned their automobiles on the center span and crawled on hands and knees along the concrete curbing, terrified that the twisting steel structure would drop into the freezing, turbulent waters below.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE PLUNGE OF THE MAIN SPAN
Standing near the east tower was camera shop owner Barney Elliott, who had arrived with a Bell and Howell sixteen-millimeter motion picture camera loaded with Kodachrome color film. Elliott began filming what would become one of the most famous and widely viewed documentary recordings in human history: capturing the bridge twisting like a rubber band against the gray November sky. A brave engineering professor named F.B. Farquharson walked out onto the twisting span in a desperate attempt to rescue Tubby the dog from Coatsworth's car. Farquharson reached the Buick and reached inside, but the terrified cocker spaniel bit him on the hand; Farquharson was forced to crawl back to safety alone. At ten-thirty, a massive six-hundred-foot section of the steel center span broke loose from its suspenders, plunging into the swirling waters of Puget Sound with a thunderous roar. Relieved of that weight, the towers whipped backward, and at eleven-oh-two in the morning, the remaining seven hundred feet of the main span unzipped, tearing itself from the cables and crashing into the depths four hundred feet below, sending colossal plumes of white spray into the air. Leonard Coatsworth attempted to reach his terrified cocker spaniel Tubby trapped in the backseat, but the violent sixty-degree tilt of the roadway threw him repeatedly against the guardrail, forcing him to crawl back to safety alone.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THEODORE VON KÁRMÁN AND AEROELASTIC FLUTTER
Miraculously, the only fatality of the Galloping Gertie collapse was poor Tubby the dog; every human on the span escaped safely. But the engineering world was shaken to its core. A federal investigation led by world-renowned aerodynamicist Theodore von Kármán discovered that the disaster was caused by an unrecognized aerodynamic phenomenon known as aeroelastic flutter: the solid eight-foot steel girders acted like airplane wings, shedding alternating vortexes of wind above and below the deck that amplified the twisting motion until structural failure occurred. The collapse forever changed bridge engineering. All future suspension bridges were tested extensively in wind tunnels, and solid plate girders were replaced by open steel trusses that allowed gale winds to pass harmlessly through. Barney Elliott sixteen-millimeter Kodachrome film reel captured the terrifying structural collapse in vivid color, providing civil engineers and physicists with unprecedented visual data that became mandatory study in every engineering curriculum.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: STURDY GERTIE AND THE UNDERWATER OCTOPUS REEF
In nineteen fifty, a new, wider Tacoma Narrows Bridge—nicknamed 'Sturdy Gertie'—was completed on the exact same site, featuring deep open-steel trusses, hydraulic dampers, and substantial structural weight that withstood the strongest Pacific gales without a shudder. In two thousand seven, a parallel suspension span was added to accommodate burgeoning traffic. Meanwhile, the ruined steel wreckage of the original Galloping Gertie still lies at the bottom of Puget Sound, four hundred feet down in the icy, swift-running tidal currents. In nineteen ninety-two, the underwater wreckage was placed on the National Register of Historic Places, recognized as one of the largest and most ecologically vibrant artificial reefs in the Pacific Northwest—a silent marine kingdom teeming with giant Pacific octopuses, wolf eels, and sea anemones that live among the twisted steel bones of history's most famous engineering failure. The replacement bridge, nicknamed Sturdy Gertie, incorporated deep open trusses and wind slots, demonstrating that modern engineering must respect the dynamic aerodynamic forces of nature rather than relying solely on static load calculations.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Galloping Gertie disaster taught civil engineers that structural strength is not just about resisting gravity, but harmonizing with the fluid forces of nature. It proves that failure, when studied with humility and science, is the greatest teacher of all. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we head to the frozen north for the Klondike Gold Rush and Seward's Folly. Until then, stay curious.
